$comment: The plot palette. Single source of truth for both projects.
Edit THIS file, then run tools/gen-palette.mjs, which regenerates
plot-web/shared/src/palette.ts and the Kotlin PlotPalette.kt. Neither
generated file should be edited by hand.
A plot's colour_index (0-7) is assigned by fieldar.pick_colour_index() so
that no two plots within 500 m share a slot. Colours are chosen to survive
the two backgrounds this app actually runs against: satellite imagery of
farmland, and a phone camera pointed at a field. Both are dominated by
green and brown, so there is no green in the palette - a green boundary on
a green crop is the one combination guaranteed to disappear. White is
included because the first field test happened after dark, where it reads
better than any hue.

alpha.$comment: Opacity each surface is drawn at, so the web tool and the AR overlay agree. Raised after field testing: the first outdoor run produced an overlay that was technically correct and practically invisible against bright soil under an overcast sky. A phone screen outdoors competes with daylight, and alpha values chosen while looking at a monitor indoors do not survive that. wallFill stays the lowest of the group because walls overlap - standing inside a plot puts four in frame at once.

$comment: Crop-health severity ramp, shared by the web map and the AR overlay.
Kept apart from the plot palette above on purpose: that palette answers
'which plot is this', this one answers 'how is the crop doing'.
Colours and alphas both raised after the first field test. The original ramp
ran green-yellow-amber-brown, chosen so the bad end described the ground
rather than alarming about it. Outdoors that reasoning failed on its own
terms: amber and brown ARE the colour of dry soil, so the two worst bands
were painting earth-colour onto earth and disappearing completely. A grading
layer has to contrast with the ground it grades, not match it.
So the bad end is now red. That does collide with plot slot 0, and the
collision is accepted rather than overlooked: the two never share a surface -
plot colour is a standing wall and a rail against the sky, severity is a flat
patch on the ground - and only one plot in eight draws in slot 0 at all.
fillAlpha still rises with severity, but from a much higher floor. Healthy
stays the faintest: it is context, and must not paint over the crop.
